analysis.title: Is Liquidity To Blame For The Sea Of Red On Your Screens?
key_insights: Excess liquidity (real money growth versus economic growth) has been falling for several months and is starting to weigh on global risk assets.
Excess liquidity operates with a three-to-six month lag, so the current period is when its impact is likely to be most noticeable.
The decline in excess liquidity is not driven by money growth. US M1 recently lifted the G10 median money growth. The cause is the lagged effect of a pick-up in growth and, more so, inflation.
Money growth cannot be read in isolation. Part is absorbed by real economic growth and part by inflation. Only the remainder is available to support markets, and that portion is small.
The framework explains why higher oil prices are ultimately negative for stocks: they raise inflation, which absorbs liquidity.
Cracks are showing in the AI trade. Proximate causes include compute overcapacity concerns, and the remote cause is the squeeze on excess liquidity.
The liquidity squeeze is unlikely to ease until monetary policy loosens or a new AI narrative revives animal spirits, unlocking more savings or boosting bank credit.
